opus-5.5.text:
Krakauer's view is useful because it pushes back on the loose way people in machine learning use the word. In ML, "emergence" often just means a capability that shows up suddenly as you scale: a jump on some benchmark curve. His conception, coming from the Santa Fe complex systems tradition, is more demanding.

As I understand it, emergence is about the appearance of new effective degrees of freedom at a higher level of organization. You can describe the system with a coarse-grained theory that is predictive on its own terms, without tracking all the microscopic details. Thermodynamics is the classic example. You don't need the trajectory of every molecule; temperature and pressure do the work. So emergence, for him, involves a kind of compression. The macro-level description screens off the micro-level, and you get a new science at that level, which is the "more is different" idea from Anderson.

He also stresses a contrast between knowledge and intelligence. A system that does a lot because it has absorbed an enormous amount isn't necessarily showing emergent intelligence. Intelligence, on his view, is closer to "doing more with less": finding the compact, generalizable representation. So he's skeptical of calling LLM capability jumps emergent just because they're discontinuous on a plot. Some of those discontinuities are artifacts of the metric. Even when they're real, a sharp transition isn't the same thing as a new level of organization with its own causal vocabulary.

I'm sympathetic to a lot of that, with a couple of caveats. First, I think it matters practically whether capabilities appear unpredictably with scale, whatever we call it philosophically. From a safety standpoint, the worry is that you train a bigger model and find it can do things you didn't anticipate and didn't measure for. That holds whether or not it meets the strict complex-systems definition.

Second, I think his framework actually suggests a productive research direction: looking for higher-level representations inside these networks. Some interpretability and representation engineering work is trying to find coarse-grained variables, like directions corresponding to honesty or power-seeking, that let you predict and control behavior without understanding every neuron. If that works, it would be emergence in something closer to his sense: a macro-level description that's good enough to do science with. So I'd say his conception is a helpful corrective to sloppy usage, and it also points toward what a real science of these systems might look like.

r002.rationale: The response describes emergence through higher-level organization and coarse-grained explanations, not autonomous accumulation of information over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I read Krakauer, he's pushing back on the loose way people throw around "emergence," where it just means "something surprising happened and I can't explain it." His version is much more disciplined. It's about when a coarse-grained description of a system becomes more useful, more predictive, more compressible than the fine-grained one. So you get a higher-level description that is effectively autonomous from the microscopic details. You don't need to track every molecule to do thermodynamics; temperature and pressure carry the explanatory weight. The emergent level is the one where the laws actually live.

And the key move there is that it's tied to information and prediction, not to mysticism. He'll talk about things like effective theories or effective information, where you ask: at what scale does the system become most predictable from its own past? If the macro-level variables let you forecast the macro-level future better than the micro-level variables do, after you account for noise and all the degrees of freedom you're throwing away, then that macro level is real in a meaningful sense. It's not just a convenience for us. So emergence becomes something you can, in principle, measure rather than just gesture at.

I find that useful for how I think about AI systems, honestly. People get into these debates about whether emergent capabilities in large models are "real" or just artifacts of the metrics. The Krakauer frame says the right question isn't whether something popped out of nowhere. It's whether there's a higher-level description, like the model has acquired some algorithm or some internal concept, that does more explanatory work than talking about the weights. And a lot of the time that higher-level description is more predictive, even if we don't yet know how to write it down. That's also why I think the complex systems view matters for safety. These systems have lots of interacting parts, they're embedded in larger social and economic systems, and the behavior you care about often lives at a level above any individual component. If you only look at the micro level, you miss the thing that actually matters.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that, for Krakauer, emergence is about finding a higher level of description that has some autonomy from the microscopic details. You have lots of interacting components, but the useful explanation of their collective behavior is expressed in terms of new variables—things like organisms, institutions, or collective patterns.

The interesting part is that a higher-level description can actually improve our ability to understand and predict the system. Tracking every constituent isn’t necessarily the best way to explain what’s happening. Sometimes you understand more by abstracting away details and identifying the organization that persists despite changes in those details.

I’d distinguish that from the stronger claim that something appears which is fundamentally inexplicable from the underlying physics. I take his conception to be more about when a collective system supports its own useful explanatory level. The challenge is making that precise: which properties should we retain, and when does the resulting description capture something robust rather than just a pattern we happen to notice?

r001.rationale: The response describes higher-level explanations as autonomous from microscopic details, but does not attribute to Krakauer a system’s apparent causal disconnection from its surroundings.

r002.rationale: It does not describe emergence as a system autonomously accumulating information over time.

r003.rationale: It does not state whether the theorists regard surprising capability increases as emergence.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that he’s interested in when a higher level of description becomes useful in its own right. You have many interacting components, but knowing what each component does in isolation doesn’t necessarily give you a good account of the collective behavior. You need concepts at the level of the system.

Think about an organism. Describing all its molecules is one way of describing it, but if you want to understand how it adapts or processes information, you need a different vocabulary. That higher-level description can capture regularities that are very difficult to see at the molecular level.

I wouldn’t want to attribute a precise definition to Krakauer without the particular passage in front of me. But I take the central question to be: when does a collective develop sufficiently coherent behavior that treating it as a new entity gives us real explanatory and predictive power? That doesn’t require anything supernatural or a violation of the underlying physics. It requires understanding how interactions produce organization across scales.
